text: LIS two ways, mountains, indexing by a property.

Longest increasing subsequence (LIS): f[i] = the longest increasing subsequence ending at a[i] = 1 + max f[j] over j < i with a[j] < a[i]. O(n²). The answer is max f[i], since it ends somewhere. a = 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6, tails g[]: after 3 1 4 1 4 after 1 5 9 1 4 5 9 after 2 1 2 5 9 after 6 1 2 5 6
O(n log n): keep g[k] = the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. g stays sorted, so each new x replaces the first g[k] ≥ x (lower_bound), or extends g.
The length of g is the answer.
A smaller tail is never worse: anything that extends a longer tail also extends a smaller one. g itself is not an actual subsequence (1 2 5 6 happens to be one here; in general it is not).

Missiles (P1020): one system intercepts a non-increasing sequence of heights. Part 1 = the longest non- increasing subsequence. Part 2 = how many systems cover all missiles = the longest strictly increasing subsequence (Dilworth's theorem: two missiles in increasing order can never share a system).
Choosing the bound: strict increase → lower_bound (equal values replace); non-strict → upper_bound (equal values extend). For decreasing versions add greater<int>() .

Chorus line (P1091): heights rise strictly to a peak and then fall strictly. Fix the peak i: the best line is (LIS ending at i) + (decreasing sequence starting at i) − 1. Two O(n²) LIS passes, one from each side.
"Best ending at i" from the left and "best starting at i" from the right, combined at i, is a common pattern for "mountain" shapes and for "split into two parts" problems.

Longest subsequence where each neighbour pair has a non-zero AND (P4310). The O(n²) DP is too slow, but "x & y ≠ 0" only depends on a shared bit, so store the best chain per bit instead of per position: O(31n).

When the transition only cares about a small property of the previous element (a bit, a remainder, a value range), index the DP by that property. The same idea speeds up LIS with a Fenwick tree over values.
Edit distance, LCS, LCS of permutations as LIS.

Two sequences: the state is a pair of prefixes, f[i][j] = the answer for a[1..i] and b[1..j]. Look at the last characters a[i] and b[j]: either they are used together, or one of them is not used at all.

Edit distance (P2758): the boundaries matter, f[i][0] = i and f[0][j] = j. Strings are 0-based, so a[i − 1] is the i-th character. O(nm) time; only the previous row is needed if memory is tight.
The same table shape solves LCS, "is b a subsequence of a", and counting ways to pick k pieces of a that concatenate to b (P2679 子串 , which adds a third index for the number of pieces).

LCS of two permutations with n = 10⁵ (P1439): O(n²) is too slow. Replace each value of b by its position in a. A common subsequence is then exactly an increasing sequence of positions, so LCS = LIS, O(n log n).
Here b becomes positions 2 1 0 3 4, whose LIS is 3 (for example 1 3 4: values 2, 4, 5). This only works because each value appears once in a.
Two walkers on a grid; counting cards.

T both walkers move at the same time: step k = x + y same cell ⇔ same x solid takes 6, dashed takes 7

Higher-dimensional states appear when several things move at once or several counters matter. Two walkers collect numbers on a grid, both moving right/down; a cell's number counts once (P1004 方格取数). Walking one after the other is wrong: the best first path can spoil the second.

Move them together: after k steps both are on the diagonal x + y = k, so the state f[k][x1][x2] fixes both cells. They share a cell exactly when x1 = x2. Four transitions (each walker came from the left or from above).
Removing a dimension: four indices (x1, y1, x2, y2) become three because y = k − x. That cuts n⁴ states to 2n·n². Unreachable states stay 0, which is safe here because all numbers are non-negative.
The same trick, "walk both paths at once", solves passing notes there and back (P1006) and the triple- experience triangle with k picks (P1544 三倍经验 adds a "uses left" index).
Tortoise chess (P1541): the state is how many cards of each kind are used. The position on the board is not a separate index: it follows from the counts, pos = a + 2b + 3c + 4d.
Rule for picking dimensions: keep everything the future depends on, and drop anything that can be computed from the rest. 40⁴ = 2.56 million states is fine; adding the position would not be.
Memory grows with every dimension: f[41][41][41][41] ints is about 11 MB, but one more index of size 350 would be 3.9 GB. Estimate the state count before writing the arrays.

Key points to memorise
1. LIS O(n²): f[i] = 1 + max f[j] (j < i, a[j] < a[i]); answer max f[i].
2. LIS O(n log n): g[k] = smallest tail of length k+1; strict → lower_bound, non-strict → upper_bound.
3. Fewest non-increasing chains = longest strictly increasing (Dilworth).
4. Mountain: best ending at i from the left + best starting at i from the right − 1.
5. Two sequences: f[i][j] on prefixes; look at a[i], b[j].
6. Edit distance: f[i][0] = i, f[0][j] = j; min(del, ins, replace/keep).
7. LCS of permutations: replace by positions, then LIS.
8. Two walkers: step k = x + y, state f[k][x1][x2], add a shared cell once.
9. Drop any index that follows from the others (position from card counts).
